# Common Pitfalls of Color Use

## Color needs a job

- Color is powerful, but poor choices can ruin a good figure
- Color must serve a purpose, be clear, and not distract
- Four pitfalls:
    - Encoding too much or irrelevant information
    - Non-monotonic color scales for data values
    - Overly saturated, gratuitous color
    - Not designing for color-vision deficiency

## Too many colors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Population growth vs. population size, 51 states, each its own color
- Matching legend to points means constant back-and-forth
- Colors are distinguishable in principle, but the task is too burdensome

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-popgrowth-colored", fig_popgrowth_colored(),
          w = 5.5, h = 7.4, x = 9.5, y = 1.2, width = 5.6)
```

## Use direct labels instead

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Qualitative scales work best with 3 to 5 categories; at 8 to 10 or more they fail
- Color by region (4 colors) and label a subset of states directly
- Leave most points unlabeled to avoid crowding

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-popgrowth-labeled", fig_popgrowth_labeled(),
          w = 5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Coloring for the sake of coloring

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- A rainbow of bars adds no information
- The colors are also too saturated: large areas of intense color pull the eye away from the labels and bar ends
- Avoid large filled areas of overly saturated color

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-popgrowth-rainbow-bars", fig_popgrowth_rainbow_bars(),
          w = 4.5, h = 5.4, x = 9.5, y = 1.3, width = 5.8)
```

## Non-monotonic color scales {.t}

- A sequential scale must show which values are larger, and by how much
- Rainbow fails both tests
- In grayscale it goes dark, light, very dark, then medium
- Its lightest third covers yellow through cyan

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-rainbow-desaturated", fig_rainbow_desaturated(),
          w = 7.14, h = 2, x = 4.5, y = 5.3, width = 11)
```

## Rainbow scales distort data

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Percent identifying as white, Texas counties
- Rainbow highlights arbitrary features of the data (here, around 75%)
- Also too saturated for comfortable viewing

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-texas-rainbow", fig_texas_rainbow(),
          w = 6, h = 4.5, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Color-vision deficiency (cvd) {.t}

- A good share of readers cannot distinguish some colors
- Sequential scales (dark to light) are generally safe
- Diverging scales are riskier: red and green look nearly identical to deutans and protans

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-red-green-cvd", fig_red_green_cvd(),
          w = 7.14, h = 2, x = 4.5, y = 5.3, width = 11)
```

## A cvd-safe diverging scale {.t}

- ColorBrewer PiYG looks red-green to most readers
- It works because the reddish end is really pink (red + blue) and the greenish end contains yellow
- The difference in blue is visible to deutans and protans

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-piyg-cvd", fig_piyg_cvd(),
          w = 7.14, h = 2, x = 4.5, y = 5.3, width = 11)
```

## The Okabe-Ito qualitative palette

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Orange #E69F00
- Sky blue #56B4E9
- Bluish green #009E73
- Yellow #F0E442
- Blue #0072B2
- Vermilion #D55E00
- Reddish purple #CC79A7
- Black #000000

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

## Safe scales are not magic

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Small elements are hard to distinguish, especially under cvd: thin lines, small points
- Large areas are easier than thin lines
- Test your figures in a cvd simulator, not just with safe palettes

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-colors-thin-lines", fig_colors_thin_lines(),
          w = 7.14, h = 5.7, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```
